name: Char Dham, Solophok
image_query: Siddhesvara Dham Char Dham Namchi Shiva statue
tagline: A 108 ft Shiva and India's four dhams on one Sikkim hilltop
meta_description: Char Dham (Siddhesvara Dham) at Solophok, Namchi: what is there, entry fee, timings, how to reach from Gangtok, and tips for pilgrims.
summary: Char Dham, officially Siddhesvara Dham, is a Hindu pilgrimage complex on Solophok hill, about 5 km from Namchi. Opened in November 2011, it has a 108 ft seated Shiva, an 18 ft Kirateshwar and replicas of the four dhams and twelve jyotirlingas, spread over roughly 29 hectares.
intro: Siddhesvara Dham sits on the flat top of Solophok hill, above the road from Namchi towards Jorethang. The complex was built by the Sikkim government and inaugurated on 8 November 2011. Its central figure, a seated Shiva painted in copper and blue tones, is 108 ft (about 33 m) high and visible from much of Namchi. Around it are full-size temple replicas of Badrinath, Jagannath Puri, Dwarka and Rameswaram.

The idea is simple: pilgrims who cannot travel to the four corners of India can make a symbolic Char Dham yatra in one morning. Twelve jyotirlinga shrines ring the Shiva statue, and there is a Sai Baba temple and a statue of Kirateshwar, Shiva as the hunter, which ties the complex to Sikkim's Kirati (Limbu and Rai) communities.

For non-pilgrims it is still worth an hour or two: the scale is surprising, the grounds are well kept and the hill gives one of the widest views in the south, across Namchi to Samdruptse and, on clear days, Kangchenjunga. Expect crowds of families on weekends and in May and October, and very few people at opening time.

story.title: Shiva the hunter: why Kirateshwar stands here
story.text: Next to the great seated Shiva at Solophok stands a smaller, 18 ft figure of Kirateshwar, Shiva in the form of a kirata, a mountain hunter. The form comes from an episode in the Mahabharata, retold in Bharavi's 6th-century poem Kiratarjuniya, in which Shiva tests the archer Arjuna disguised as a hunter before granting him a divine weapon. In Sikkim the form has a local home: the Kirateshwar Mahadev temple at Legship on the Rangeet, in Gyalshing district, where, as told locally, Arjuna did his penance. The name also echoes the Kirati peoples, the Limbu and Rai, whose communities have long lived in Sikkim's southern and western hills. Placing Kirateshwar at Siddhesvara Dham alongside the pan-Indian four dhams was a deliberate nod to those roots, so that the complex speaks to Sikkim's own Hindu and Kirati traditions, not only to pilgrims from the plains.

little_known.fact: The complex spreads over about 29 hectares on Solophok hill, which is why the four dham replicas can stand at full temple scale rather than as small models.
The seated Shiva is 108 ft tall, a number sacred in Hindu and Buddhist practice, the same count as the beads on a prayer mala.
Solophok's Shiva and Samdruptse's Guru Rinpoche, on opposite hills across Namchi, were completed seven years apart, in 2011 and 2004.

facts: 108 ft Shiva, four dham replicas, 12 jyotirlingas

highlights.title: The 108 ft seated Shiva
highlights.text: The central statue, about 33 m tall, sits on a broad plinth with a temple inside. Walk around it clockwise as pilgrims do. Morning light from the east falls on its face; afternoon light is better for photographing the replicas.

highlights.title: Four dhams in one morning
highlights.text: Replicas of Badrinath, Jagannath Puri, Dwarka and Rameswaram stand around the hilltop, each with priests and daily worship. Many families from the plains do the full round of all four with offerings.

highlights.title: Twelve jyotirlinga shrines
highlights.text: Small shrines for the twelve jyotirlingas, from Somnath to Kedarnath, ring the main statue. Each has a board explaining its original location in India, useful for children.

highlights.title: Kirateshwar statue
highlights.text: An 18 ft figure of Shiva as the hunter, linked to the Kirateshwar Mahadev temple at Legship and to Sikkim's Kirati communities. One of the few places on a pan-Indian pilgrimage route with a local Sikkim twist.

highlights.title: Views over Namchi
highlights.text: From the edge of the complex you look across Namchi to Samdruptse's Guru Rinpoche, and north to Kangchenjunga on clear mornings. The best panoramic photo is from the parking-side terrace.

how_to_reach.text: Take a shared jeep to Namchi from Gangtok (about ₹250–350) or Siliguri (about ₹300–400), then a local taxi up to Solophok, roughly 5 km and 15 minutes, for about ₹300–500 return with waiting. Some Namchi–Jorethang shared jeeps drop at the turn-off, but the walk up is steep.

Most visitors include Char Dham in a Namchi sightseeing loop with Samdruptse and the Rock Garden, about ₹2,000–3,000 for a half day. From Gangtok, a day trip covering Namchi and Char Dham costs roughly ₹4,500–6,000 by small car.

Solophok is about 95–100 km from Bagdogra and NJP, 3.5–4 hours by car via Melli and Namchi. Pilgrims arriving by train often visit Char Dham on the way up and sleep in Namchi. If NH10 is closed, cars use the Darjeeling–Jorethang road.

where_to_stay: There is no hotel on the hill itself; stay in Namchi, 5 km away. Sobralia Hotels Casino Resort & Spa is on the road up to Char Dham and the closest upmarket option. Seven Hill Resort at Phalidara has cottages that look across to the Shiva statue. Budget hotels around Namchi's Central Park cost about ₹1,500–2,500 a room and are fine for pilgrims on a tight budget.
tips: Arrive at opening time (around 8 am) to have the complex almost to yourself.
Shoes come off at every shrine; carry socks for cold marble in winter.
Leather belts and bags are best left in the car.
Wheelchairs and slow walkers manage most paths; a few shrines have steps.
Combine with Samdruptse on the opposite hill for a two-faith morning in Namchi.

experiences.title: A Char Dham yatra in two hours
experiences.summary: Walk the full round of Siddhesvara Dham as pilgrims do: the four dham replicas, twelve jyotirlingas and the great Shiva, with time for a small puja. Unhurried, respectful and best early, before the day's buses arrive from Gangtok.
body: The Char Dham of Hindu tradition are Badrinath in the north, Jagannath Puri in the east, Rameswaram in the south and Dwarka in the west. Visiting all four is a lifetime aim for many families. At Solophok, each has a replica temple with resident priests, so a pilgrimage that takes weeks across India can be done in a morning.

Start at the main gate, walk clockwise around the hilltop and visit each dham in turn, then the ring of twelve jyotirlinga shrines around the central Shiva. Priests will offer to perform a short puja; a donation of ₹51–201 is customary but not compulsory. Flowers and prasad are sold near the entrance.

Finish inside the plinth of the Shiva statue, then at the Kirateshwar figure. Allow two hours at a pilgrim's pace. Mornings are quietest; Mondays and Shivratri bring crowds. Keep voices low near the sanctums and ask before photographing priests or rituals.

faqs.q: Do the priests expect a fee?
faqs.a: There is no fixed fee for darshan beyond the entry ticket. If you ask a priest to perform a puja, a donation is customary, usually ₹51–201. You can decline politely. Donation boxes are at each shrine for those who prefer to give anonymously.

faqs.q: Is Char Dham crowded on Shivratri?
faqs.a: Yes. Maha Shivratri (February or March) and Mondays in the Hindu month of Shravan (July–August) bring large crowds of local and visiting devotees. If you want quiet, avoid those days. If you want atmosphere, go, but arrive very early and expect slow traffic.

faqs.q: Can non-Hindus visit Char Dham?
faqs.a: Yes, visitors of all faiths are welcome in the complex. Dress modestly, remove shoes at shrines and follow the priests' guidance inside sanctums. Some inner areas may be reserved for worship during aarti; simply wait or watch from outside.

experiences.title: Evening aarti on Solophok hill
experiences.summary: Stay on at Char Dham for the evening lamp ceremony, when bells ring across the hilltop and the Shiva statue is lit against the dusk. A quieter, more local experience than the midday crowds, best combined with sunset over the Darjeeling ridge.
body: Aarti, the offering of lamps, is performed at the shrines around dusk. Priests circle flames before the deities while bells and conch shells sound, and local families who live near Solophok come up for darshan after work. It is short, about 20–30 minutes, and free to watch.

Arrive an hour before sunset to walk the grounds as the light turns gold, then find a place near the main shrine. On clear evenings the sun sets over the Darjeeling hills to the south-west and the statue is lit soon after. Timings move with the season, so ask at the gate in the morning or call your hotel.

Book your taxi for the return trip in advance, as few cars wait at the top after dark. Bring a warm layer: the hilltop is breezy and evenings cool quickly, even in April. Closing time is usually around 6 pm, so confirm that aarti falls within opening hours on your date.

faqs.q: What time is aarti at Char Dham?
faqs.a: Evening aarti is held around dusk, which ranges from about 5 pm in winter to 6:30 pm in summer. Timings change and depend on the complex's opening hours, which have been roughly 8 am to 6 pm. Ask at the gate or check with your hotel the same day.

faqs.q: Is there transport back to Namchi in the evening?
faqs.a: Not reliably. Few taxis wait at the top after dark, so ask your driver to wait or come back at a fixed time. A return trip from Namchi with an hour's wait costs about ₹300–500. Shared jeeps pass on the main road below but the walk down is steep.

faqs.q: Can we photograph the aarti?
faqs.a: Photography of the outside of the complex and the lit statue is generally fine. During the ritual, avoid flash and do not stand in front of priests or worshippers. Inside sanctums, ask first. A phone in night mode does a good job of the statue after dark.

experiences.title: Two-statue panorama from Solophok
experiences.summary: On a clear morning, the terraces at Solophok frame Namchi town, Samdruptse's gilded Guru Rinpoche on the opposite hill and the white line of Kangchenjunga behind. A short photography session that gives the best single view of the district.
body: Solophok is one of the highest points close to Namchi, and its north-facing edge looks straight across the town to Samdruptse, about 7 km away in a straight line. With a moderate zoom you can frame the Guru Rinpoche statue against the hills, and on clear days Kangchenjunga and its neighbours rise above the far ridge.

The light is best in the first two hours after opening, when the sun is behind you to the east and the haze has not yet built up. October to February is the clearest season. In spring, haze often softens the view by 10 am; in the monsoon, low cloud can sit below the hilltop, which makes for a different kind of picture.

Use the parking-side terrace and the paths behind the four dham replicas for clean angles. Tripods are usually fine outdoors; be considerate of pilgrims. Combine the session with the Char Dham walk, then drive to Samdruptse for the reverse view in the late morning.

faqs.q: Can we see Kangchenjunga from Char Dham?
faqs.a: Yes, on clear days, mostly October to February and some spring mornings. The mountain rises above the ridges to the north-west. Arrive early; by late morning haze or cloud usually builds. In the monsoon months it is rarely visible.

faqs.q: Are drones allowed at Char Dham?
faqs.a: Assume not without permission. Religious complexes and parts of Sikkim near sensitive areas restrict drone flying, and rules are enforced. Ask the management office at the gate and check current status before you travel. A phone or camera with a short zoom covers the views well.

faqs.q: What lens is useful for this view?
faqs.a: A wide lens for the complex itself and a moderate zoom, around 70–200 mm equivalent, to bring Samdruptse and the mountains closer. Phone users should use the 2x or 3x setting for the statue across the valley and step back from railings to avoid reflections.

experiences.title: Pilgrim's vegetarian lunch after the yatra
experiences.summary: After the morning round at Siddhesvara Dham, eat a simple vegetarian thali at the canteens near the gate or in Namchi town: rice, dal, seasonal sabzi, pickle and curd. Cheap, filling and a taste of the plains-meets-hills food that the pilgrims brought.
body: Char Dham draws pilgrims from Bihar, Bengal, Assam and beyond, and the food around it has followed: pure-vegetarian canteens near the complex and in Namchi serve rice, roti, dal, a seasonal vegetable, pickle, papad and sometimes kheer. A full thali costs about ₹150–300 and refills of rice and dal are usually included.

In the hills the sabzi changes with the season: squash and its shoots in summer, mustard greens and radish in winter, local beans in autumn. Some places add a Sikkimese touch with a side of gundruk, fermented leafy greens, or a small bowl of dalle chilli pickle. Ask for it if you like heat.

Eat early, from noon, before the coaches arrive. Most canteens take UPI and cash. If you prefer to sit longer, drive back to Namchi's Central Park, where several vegetarian restaurants serve thalis, dosas and North Indian dishes in a quieter setting.

faqs.q: Is food at Char Dham pure vegetarian?
faqs.a: The canteens and stalls inside and next to the complex are vegetarian, in keeping with the pilgrimage. Onion and garlic may be used in some dishes; ask if you follow a satvik diet. Namchi town has both vegetarian and non-vegetarian restaurants.

faqs.q: What is gundruk?
faqs.a: Gundruk is fermented and dried leafy greens, usually mustard, radish or cauliflower leaves, made across Nepali-speaking communities in Sikkim. It has a sour, earthy taste and is cooked into soups or pickles. It is often served with rice in winter.

faqs.q: Can we get Jain food near Char Dham?
faqs.a: Strict Jain food (no root vegetables) is not standard, but some vegetarian restaurants in Namchi will prepare it if you ask in advance. Tell us when you book and we will call ahead. Carry some dry snacks in case options are limited on the road.

faqs.q: What is Char Dham in Namchi?
faqs.a: Char Dham, officially Siddhesvara Dham, is a Hindu pilgrimage complex on Solophok hill near Namchi, opened in November 2011. It has a 108 ft seated Shiva, an 18 ft Kirateshwar, replicas of the four dhams (Badrinath, Jagannath, Dwarka, Rameswaram) and the twelve jyotirlingas, so pilgrims can make a symbolic yatra in one place.

faqs.q: What is the entry fee for Char Dham, Namchi?
faqs.a: The entry fee has been about ₹50 per adult, with parking around ₹30–50 per car. Children usually pay less. Fees are revised from time to time, so check current status before you travel. Offerings and puja donations are separate and voluntary.

faqs.q: What are Char Dham's opening hours?
faqs.a: The complex has generally opened around 8 am and closed around 6 pm, every day. Timings can shift by season and on festival days. Arrive at opening time for the quietest visit and the clearest views of Kangchenjunga.

faqs.q: How far is Char Dham from Namchi town?
faqs.a: About 5 km, 15 minutes by car. Taxis from Namchi charge roughly ₹300–500 for a return trip with an hour's waiting. Walking up is possible but steep and busy with traffic, so most visitors drive.

faqs.q: How much time do we need at Char Dham?
faqs.a: Allow 1.5–2 hours to walk the full round of the four dhams, the jyotirlinga shrines and the main statue at a relaxed pace. Pilgrims doing puja at each shrine may take 3 hours. Add 30 minutes for photos from the terraces.

faqs.q: Is Char Dham suitable for elderly visitors?
faqs.a: Yes, mostly. Paths are broad and paved, with ramps and some steps. Benches are placed around the grounds. Wheelchair users can see most of the complex, though a few shrines involve steps. The altitude, about 1,700 m, is gentle.

faqs.q: Can we visit Char Dham as a day trip from Gangtok?
faqs.a: Yes. Namchi and Char Dham are about 3.5 hours each way, so a long day trip is possible: leave Gangtok by 7 am, see Char Dham and Samdruptse, return by 7 pm. It is more relaxed to stay a night in Namchi and add Temi or Ravangla.

faqs.q: Is photography allowed at Char Dham?
faqs.a: Photography is generally allowed in the grounds and of the statues from outside. Inside sanctums and during rituals, ask the priest first and avoid flash. Drones need permission and are usually not allowed. Be considerate of worshippers when framing shots.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit Char Dham?
faqs.a: October to December for clear skies and views of Kangchenjunga, and March to May for warm, pleasant days. Maha Shivratri and Shravan Mondays bring big crowds of devotees. Monsoon visits (June to September) are possible but often cloudy, with occasional road slides.
